guide.title: Gynecologic Emergencies
guide.lead: Anyone who could be pregnant and has abdominal pain, fainting or shock has a ruptured ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise. Treat the shock rather than chase the diagnosis. After an assault, care for the person first and protect the evidence second.

sections.title: Could this be a ruptured ectopic?
sections.question: Of childbearing age with lower abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding or fainting – and could be pregnant (missed period, even on contraception)?
sections.yes: Treat as a ruptured ectopic: lie flat, oxygen to target, IV, nothing by mouth, rapid transport, pre-alert. Shoulder-tip pain (Kehr's sign) and shock mean blood in the abdomen.
sections.no: Still think of ovarian torsion, pelvic infection, a ruptured cyst, appendicitis and kidney stones.

sections.title: Pelvic pain: what fits?
rows: Missed period (often 6–8 weeks), one-sided pain, spotting, shoulder-tip pain, fainting
Bleeding and cramps before 20 weeks; tissue passed
Count pads, bring any tissue, support
Sudden severe one-sided pain that comes in waves, vomiting, can't keep still
Pain on both sides, fever, discharge, pain on movement or during sex
Antibiotics; untreated it causes infertility and ectopic pregnancy
Sudden pain, often mid-cycle or after sex or exercise

sections.title: Vaginal bleeding: always ask
items: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
How many pads, and how fast are they soaking?
Blood thinners or a bleeding disorder?

steps.title: Safety and injuries first
steps.text: Make the scene safe and treat injuries. Police if the patient wants it or the law requires it.

steps.title: Consent and control
steps.text: Explain everything and ask before touching. Offer a provider of the gender they prefer when you can.

steps.title: Protect evidence
steps.text: Ask them not to wash, change, eat, drink, brush teeth or urinate if possible. Put removed clothing in separate paper bags. Don't examine the genitals unless bleeding is severe.

steps.title: Document
steps.text: Their words in quotes, injuries described objectively, who handled each item of evidence.

steps.title: Destination
steps.text: A centre with a forensic examiner. HIV prevention must start within 72 hours; emergency contraception works up to 120 hours, better the earlier it is given.

steps.title: Reporting
steps.text: Adults usually decide whether to report. Children and vulnerable adults are reported according to local law.

sections.title: Don't
items: Rely on a negative home pregnancy test when the story fits an ectopic
Throw away passed tissue: bring it in a clean container

quiz.q: 24-year-old: sudden left lower abdominal pain, spotting, light-headed, 'might be pregnant', BP 86/54, HR 124, left shoulder pain. Most likely?
quiz.explanation: Shoulder-tip pain (Kehr's sign) and shock mean blood in the abdomen: rapid transport.

quiz.q: Pain on both sides of the lower abdomen, fever, discharge, pain when the cervix is moved. Most likely?
After a sexual assault she asks to wash and change before hospital. You:
options: Explain that washing destroys evidence, offer a blanket, and let her decide
Wait for police before any care
quiz.explanation: Treat injuries first; preserve evidence where you can; she keeps control.

options: Shoulder-tip pain from blood under the diaphragm
quiz.explanation: In a woman of childbearing age with abdominal pain, think ruptured ectopic.

options: About 6–8 weeks after the last period
quiz.explanation: Often before she knows she is pregnant.

quiz.q: Sudden severe one-sided pain coming in waves, vomiting, writhing, normal temperature. Suspect:
quiz.explanation: A surgical emergency: the ovary loses its blood supply.

quiz.q: She passed tissue during a miscarriage. You:
options: Bring it to hospital in a clean container
quiz.explanation: The hospital checks whether the miscarriage is complete.

quiz.q: HIV prevention after sexual assault must start within:
quiz.explanation: So go to a centre that can start it.

quiz.q: Heavy vaginal bleeding with shock. Which is wrong?
quiz.explanation: Don't pack; use external pads and count them.

quiz.q: Removed clothing after an assault goes into:
quiz.explanation: Plastic traps moisture and degrades evidence.

flashcards.question: Ectopic pregnancy: classic triad
flashcards.answer: Missed period, abdominal or pelvic pain, vaginal bleeding. Rupture causes shock, fainting and shoulder-tip pain (Kehr's sign).

flashcards.question: Kehr's sign
flashcards.answer: Shoulder-tip pain from blood irritating the diaphragm. With abdominal pain in a woman of childbearing age: ruptured ectopic (or spleen).

flashcards.question: Evidence after sexual assault
flashcards.answer: Treat injuries first. Ask the patient not to wash, change, eat, drink or urinate if possible; separate paper bags for clothing; quote their words; record who handled evidence; centre with a forensic examiner.

flashcards.question: Pelvic inflammatory disease
flashcards.answer: Infection of the uterus, tubes and ovaries, usually chlamydia or gonorrhoea: lower abdominal pain, pain on moving the cervix, fever, discharge.

flashcards.question: Ovarian torsion
flashcards.answer: The ovary twists on its blood supply: sudden severe one-sided pain, vomiting, often in waves. Time-critical surgery.

flashcards.question: Leading cause of maternal death in the first trimester
flashcards.answer: Ruptured ectopic pregnancy. Abdominal pain or fainting in anyone who could be pregnant is ectopic until proven otherwise.

flashcards.question: Types of miscarriage
flashcards.answer: Threatened, inevitable, incomplete, complete, missed. You can't tell them apart in the field: treat the bleeding, bring any tissue, support.

flashcards.question: Reporting sexual assault
flashcards.answer: Adults usually decide whether to report. Suspected abuse of children or vulnerable adults must be reported according to local law.

critical.scenario: 20-year-old, sudden right lower abdominal pain for 2 hours, vomited twice, guarding. BP 106/68, HR 118. Last period 6 weeks ago (usually regular); on the pill.
critical.question: What must you rule out first, and how?

options.t: Ectopic pregnancy: treat as time-critical – oxygen to target, IV, nothing by mouth, rapid transport, pre-alert for ultrasound

options.f: A missed period makes ectopic the first concern.
Contraception can fail; ectopic risk remains.

critical.explanation: Appendicitis is possible, but ectopic rupture can kill within the hour.
critical.kpi: Considers ectopic pregnancy in a woman of childbearing age with abdominal pain

critical.scenario: 10 weeks pregnant: heavy bleeding with clots since morning; passed tissue 30 minutes ago and saved it. BP 108/72 lying, 92/60 sitting, HR 116.
critical.question: Diagnosis and management?

options.t: Miscarriage with significant blood loss: lie her flat, IV, count pads, bring the tissue, recheck vital signs, emotional support, transport

options.f: Postural drop and tachycardia mean real blood loss.

critical.explanation: Acknowledge the loss; many patients blame themselves.
critical.kpi: Manages miscarriage with hemodynamic compromise and provides emotional support

critical.scenario: 30-year-old, sudden severe left lower abdominal pain for 3 hours, coming in waves, vomiting, pacing. Negative pregnancy test yesterday; normal period 2 weeks ago. BP 118/76, HR 102, afebrile.
critical.question: Most likely diagnosis and plan?

options.t: Ovarian torsion: rapid transport to a hospital with gynaecology, analgesia per protocol, nothing by mouth

options.f: Possible, but torsion must be excluded urgently.

options.t: Wait to see if it settles
options.f: Every hour reduces the chance of saving the ovary.

critical.explanation: Partial twisting and untwisting makes the pain come in waves.
critical.kpi: Recognizes ovarian torsion as a time-sensitive surgical emergency
